A.explanation: This is $-3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, a loss or gain of 3 whole electrons, so it is a possible ion charge.

B.explanation: This is $+1 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, the charge of a singly ionised positive ion, so it is possible.

C.explanation: This is $+2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, the charge of a doubly ionised positive ion, so it is possible.

D.explanation: This is $2.5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, which is not a whole number of elementary charges and so cannot occur.

hints: Look at the size of each charge in $\text{C}$ - they are all a few times $10^{-19} \text{ C}$, so compare each to the elementary charge $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Recall charge quantisation for ions in an electrolyte: the charge must be $Q = \pm ne$ where $n = 1, 2, 3...$ is a whole number of electrons lost or gained.
Divide each listed value by $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and check which one does not give a positive or negative integer.
walkthrough: Identify the rule: charge is quantised, so any ion in solution must have charge $Q = ne$ where $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and $n$ is an integer, positive for loss of electrons and negative for gain.
Test each value by calculating $n = Q/e$. For $-4.8 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $n = -4.8/1.6 = -3$, a whole number.
For $+1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $n = +1.6/1.6 = +1$, and for $+3.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $n = +3.2/1.6 = +2$, both whole numbers and therefore possible.
For $+4.0 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $n = +4.0/1.6 = +2.5$, which is not an integer and would require half an electron, which is impossible. This is option D.
